hints: Look at the position of each label in Fig. 9.1. A is right in the centre surrounded by many spiral layers, while B is a small shaded oval sitting in the outer wrapping layer - what part of a neurone is always in the middle, and what cell makes the wrapping?

Remember that myelin is made by a Schwann cell wrapping its membrane many times around the conducting fibre. The conducting fibre contains cytoplasm, and the wrapping cell still keeps its own control centre pushed to the outside.
walkthrough:
Read the spiral as a wrapping**
Think of the diagram as a Schwann cell rolling its cell surface membrane many times around a central fibre. The many concentric rings are layers of myelin membrane, so everything inside the rings must be the fibre being wrapped and everything in the outer layer belongs to the wrapping cell.

Name A and B**
The central fibre that carries the action potential is the axon, and the cytoplasm inside it is axoplasm, so A is axon / axoplasm. The dark oval in the outer cytoplasm of the wrapping cell is where its DNA is kept, so B is the Schwann cell nucleus.
Final answer: A - axon / axoplasm; B - Schwann cell nucleus.

hints: Start by deciding which neurone is faster overall, then ask where $Na^{+}$ influx can actually happen if thick myelin covers most of the axon membrane.
Recall that depolarisation to threshold and opening of voltage-gated $Na^{+}$ channels happen together. If channels are missing under myelin, where must depolarisation be renewed?
Think about local circuits between a depolarised region and the next resting region. How does insulation by myelin affect how far the charge can spread before leaking out?
Link the jumping of the action potential from gap to gap to its special name, and be ready to state clearly that myelinated conduction is faster.
walkthrough:
Place the channels**
Voltage-gated $Na^{+}$ channels are proteins in the axon membrane that open when depolarisation reaches threshold and let $Na^{+}$ rush in. In a non-myelinated neurone they are spread along the whole length of the membrane. In a myelinated neurone myelin insulates the membrane, so functional channels are concentrated only at the gaps called nodes of Ranvier.

Decide where depolarisation is renewed**
Influx of $Na^{+}$ causes the reversal of charge called depolarisation. That means in a non-myelinated neurone depolarisation and a new action potential must be generated at every point along the axon. In a myelinated neurone depolarisation and regeneration occur only at the nodes.

Compare local circuits and speed**
Between one action potential and the next resting region, positive charge flows in a local circuit. Myelin prevents leakage of ions, so charge spreads further and local circuits are long. Without myelin, leakage is greater and local circuits are short, so many more slow steps are needed.

Name saltatory conduction and conclude**
Because the impulse appears to jump from node to node, myelinated conduction is called saltatory conduction. Fewer regenerations over longer distances makes transmission much faster in the myelinated neurone, about $100 m s^{-1}$ compared with about $2 m s^{-1}$ in a non-myelinated neurone.

Final answer: Myelinated neurone transmits action potential faster. In myelinated neurone voltage-gated $Na^{+}$ channels occur only at nodes of Ranvier, in non-myelinated they occur along whole length; depolarisation occurs only at nodes vs along whole length; long local circuits in myelinated vs short local circuits in non-myelinated; saltatory conduction in myelinated neurone.
